blocks.text: Some plants supplement organic molecules into their food in addition to inorganic nutrients. These organic chemicals are acquired through the process of capturing and breaking down insects and tiny animals. All insectivorous plants are true autotrophs. However, their development accelerates when they capture prey. Apparently, nitrogenous compounds of animal body are of benefit to these plants. The captured insects are broken down by enzymes that are released by the leaves. Pitcher plant, Venus fly trap and sundew are some of the known insectivorous plants.

Pitcher plant has leaves modified into a sac or a pitcher, partly filled with water (Fig.8.1). The leaf's terminal portion is altered to create a hood, which partially covers the exposed opening of the pitcher. It has numerous stiff hairs that prevent little insects from crawling out once they fall inside it.

blocks.alt: Two pictures side by side. Left: a pitcher plant's pitcher hanging from its curled tendril against a blurred pink and brown background; the speckled brown-green pitcher has a green and red rim and a large pale lid above its mouth. Right: the mouth of a pale yellow-green pitcher against a black background, its flat lid held above the opening and dark trapped insects at the rim.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.1: Pitcher plant, insects are entrapped within the leaf (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.1).

blocks.text: Venus-fly trap has a "trap" consisting of two lobes that are hinged at the end of each leaf. The inner surfaces of the lobes contain trichomes, which are hair-like projections that trigger the lobes to close rapidly upon contact with prey (Fig.8.2). The hinged traps are lined with fine bristles that interlock upon closure, preventing the prey from escaping. The trapped insect is then digested by the enzymes secreted from the glands on the leaf surface and the products are then absorbed.

blocks.alt: Two pictures side by side. Left: three traps on their leaf stalks against a dark green background; the two outer traps are open, with red inner surfaces and long bristles along their edges, and the middle trap has nearly closed on a trapped insect. Right: a close-up of a trap closing on a wasp, with other pale green traps around it.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.2: Venus-fly trap, prey is trapped between the lobes of a leaf (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.2).

blocks.text: Sundew catches its prey with shiny drops of "dew," where the plant's common name comes from (Fig. 8.3). The leaves are covered with tiny hairs that look like tentacles. Each leaf has gland and has a single drop of dew at the tip. The insects, attracted by plant's odour are trapped by tentacles. The trapped insects are digested by enzymes and products are absorbed.

blocks.alt: Two pictures side by side. Left: a round sundew leaf seen from above against an olive background, its yellow-green tentacles spreading out with red gland tips, and an insect with an orange-red thorax and a dark body caught on the tentacles. Right: a sundew leaf curled round its prey, with red tentacles inside it and many more red, dew-tipped tentacles behind.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.3: Sundew, insects are entangled by the tentacles (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.3).
